introduction-the-velocity-trap.core: Teams that weigh every decision equally get stuck in decision paralysis. Bezos's framework separates cheap-to-reverse decisions (Type 2) from costly ones (Type 1) so you can move fast on most and be careful on few.

first_principles.problem: Choosing a logging library gets the same multi-day debate as choosing the company's main database. Meetings, polls and comparison docs feel responsible, but features ship late and engineers learn to fear change.
truths: Most decisions are cheap to undo.
A few decisions are very expensive to undo.
derivation: Classify by **reversal cost**, not by how important it feels.
**Type 2** (two-way door): decide fast, learn from reality.
**Type 1** (one-way door): slow down and analyse.
Match process weight to decision type.

analogy.title: Doors in a building
analogy.story: Most doors swing both ways: walk through, look, walk back. A few lock behind you. You only need to stop and think before the locking ones.
analogy.breaks: Real doors are labelled. Decisions aren't, so assessing reversibility is the skill.

example.title: A week arguing over a log library
example.scenario: Five engineers debate two logging libraries for a week.
example.outcome: decisions that don't matter much stop eating weeks.

points: Fast on Type 2, careful on Type 1.

check.a: It's cheap and quick to reverse if it turns out wrong.

the-two-way-door-type-2-reversible-decis.core: A Type 2 decision is a two-way door: low reversal cost, small blast radius. Trying it teaches you more than debating it, so decide quickly and close to the work.

first_principles.problem: Spending three days debating something you could undo in three minutes is a net loss, even if the debate finds a slightly better answer.
truths: Undo is cheap: git revert, flag toggle, config change.
Delay often costs more than a suboptimal choice.
derivation: Check: **reversal cost low? blast radius small?**
If yes, let the **individual or team decide**.
**Try, measure, revert** if needed.

analogy.title: A restaurant swing door
analogy.story: You push through, look around, and if you don't like it, push back. You lost a few seconds.
analogy.breaks: A door costs nothing to reopen. Some 'reversible' changes leave residue (data written in a new format), so check that too.

example.title: Switching a test runner
example.scenario: An engineer wants to move one service from Mocha to Vitest.

steps.label: Assess
steps.detail: One service, revertible with a git revert.

steps.label: Act
steps.detail: No approvals needed; post an FYI.

example.outcome: the improvement ships in a day instead of after a committee.

check.q: Why is debating Type 2 decisions harmful?
check.a: The time spent costs more than any gain, and real-world trial would answer the question faster.

the-one-way-door-type-1-irreversible-dec.core: A Type 1 decision is a one-way door: reversal needs re-architecture, migrations, contracts or retraining. These deserve slow, careful, written analysis.

first_principles.problem: Primary database, cloud provider, service boundaries, public API shapes: once chosen, everything above depends on them. Choosing hastily locks in years of cost.
truths: Foundations shape everything built on them.
You often can't fully test before committing.
derivation: Identify Type 1 by **reversal mechanism and cost** (migrations, contracts).
Invest in **analysis**: requirements, options, prototypes.
Write it down (**ADR/RFC**) and involve the people affected.

analogy.title: Pouring concrete
analogy.story: Once the foundation sets, you can build on it or demolish at huge cost, but never un-pour it.
mapping: Code and data depending on it
analogy.breaks: Concrete is obviously permanent. Software looks changeable, which is why Type 1 decisions get made casually.

example.title: Choosing the primary database
example.scenario: A new product needs a database for orders and payments.

steps.label: Requirements
steps.detail: Strong consistency, 5k writes/s, team knows SQL.

example.outcome: a foundational choice made with evidence and recorded for future readers.

check.a: Primary database engine, cloud provider, and a public API contract used by customers.

the-spectrum-not-a-binary.core: Reversibility is a spectrum. Instead of arguing about the label, ask four questions: how is it reversed, how long would that take, who is affected, and does it get harder over time?

first_principles.problem: Teams debate whether something is 'Type 1 or Type 2' instead of measuring the real cost of being wrong.
truths: Reversal ranges from seconds to years.
Blast radius ranges from one team to all customers.
derivation: Ask **reversal mechanism**: revert, flag, migration, contract?
Ask **reversal time**: seconds → years.
Ask **who's affected**: team, company, customers.
Ask **does it compound?** (more data, more dependents over time).

analogy.title: Commitment levels in a relationship
analogy.story: A first coffee is trivially reversible, moving in together less so, buying a house together much less. Each step is a point on a spectrum.
analogy.breaks: Relationships progress visibly. Technical lock-in creeps in silently as data and dependents grow.

example.title: Picking a message queue
example.scenario: Is choosing Kafka vs RabbitMQ Type 1 or Type 2?

steps.label: Now
steps.detail: Only one producer, so cheap to change.

steps.label: Later
steps.detail: Dependents grow, so reversal gets costly.

example.outcome: you weigh how reversal cost will change over time, not just today.

check.a: A decision that's cheap to reverse today may become expensive as more code and data depend on it.

techniques-to-convert-type-1-decisions-i.core: Great engineers make irreversible decisions reversible: feature flags, abstraction layers, strangler patterns, parallel runs and pilots turn one-way doors into two-way doors.

first_principles.problem: Some decisions look irreversible, like launching a new pricing engine or migrating a database. Without escape hatches you must be perfect on the first try.
truths: Decoupling deploy from release makes rollback a toggle.
derivation: **Feature flags**: enable for 1%, observe, toggle off instantly.
**Abstraction layers**: code against an interface, not a vendor.
**Incremental migration** (strangler, dual-writes) instead of a big bang.
**Pilots / canaries** before full commitment.

analogy.title: Trying on before buying
analogy.story: A store with a generous return policy turns a big purchase into a reversible one. You can commit with much less analysis.
analogy.breaks: Return policies are free to you. Escape hatches cost engineering time, so build them where reversal cost is high.

example.title: Launching a new pricing engine
example.scenario: Switching pricing for all customers is risky.

steps.label: Observe
steps.detail: Compare conversion and errors against the legacy engine.

steps.label: Decide
steps.detail: Ramp to 100% or turn off in seconds.

example.outcome: a scary launch becomes a reversible experiment.

points: Spend effort where reversal is costly.

check.q: How does a feature flag change a decision's type?
check.a: It separates deploying from launching, so turning the feature off is a toggle instead of a new deploy.

determining-approval-thresholds.core: Match process weight to decision type: no approval for small reversible changes, an FYI for moderate ones, a light review for hard-to-reverse ones, and a full RFC with a deadline only for big irreversible ones.

first_principles.problem: Needing three approvals to change a log level is bureaucracy; letting one person pick the company database alone is recklessness. Both come from using one process for every decision.
truths: Process has a cost in time and morale.
Risk depends on reversal cost and impact.
derivation: **Type 2, low impact**: individual decides.
**Type 2, moderate**: inform, don't ask (Slack FYI).
**Type 1, moderate**: one senior review in 1–2 days.
**Type 1, high**: RFC/ADR with a comment period and a decision deadline.

analogy.title: Spending limits at a company
analogy.story: Small purchases need no approval, medium ones need a manager, big ones need the board. Nobody needs the board to buy a stapler.
analogy.breaks: Money is easy to measure. Reversal cost is a judgement call, so publish examples of each tier.

example.title: A team's decision tiers

steps.label: Deadline
steps.detail: RFCs close after a set comment period.

example.outcome: most work flows freely and the few big decisions get real scrutiny.

points: Inform, don't ask, for moderate Type 2.

check.q: What's the main failure mode this prevents?
check.a: Applying a heavy Type 1 approval process to cheap Type 2 decisions, which creates bureaucracy and slows everyone.
